newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: SLOVAK POSTPRIVATISATION FUND SEEKS 30 FIRMS.
newsitem.headline: SLOVAK POSTPRIVATISATION FUND SEEKS 30 FIRMS.

text.p: The Slovak Post Privatisation Fund (SPPF), which is majority-owned by the European Bank for the Reconstruction and Development (EBRD), is seeking to invest in 30 medium-sized companies, a fund official said on Thursday.
Managers of the fund hope that it will help to wake up foreign investors to opportunities in Slovakia, which has suffered from political turbulence and U-turns in the privatisation programme.

The fund, which is managed by Framlington/CET Managers Ltd and was set up earlier this year, is 69 percent-owned by the EBRD with three percent held by the European Commission and 28 percent by the government's Slovak Foundation.
"We are here to find 30 medium-sized companies, private or privatised, that we can help to develop and grow," said Framlington/CET Managing Director Andre Wavre.

"One can only achieve so much with 30 companies, but it is more than that," he told Reuters. "If we are successful -- and we will be -- it would open eyes to many, attracting more money to the country," he said.
The SPPF is a 10-year, 1.8 billion crown equity fund, of which 1.6 billion crowns is to be invested in the companies through their share increase, and the remaining 200 million on the assistance.

Foreign direct investment in Slovakia between January 1990 and June 1996 totalled a mere $808.4 million, compared with $11 billion in neighbouring Hungary and $5.0 billion in former federation partner the Czech Republic.

"In Western Europe people have the feeling that Slovakia has only farmers and its industry is in a shape about which nothing can be done," Wavre said. "It is not true, a lot of things are happening here."

The SPPF requires firms of about 200-2,000 employees which have a solid investment project of 15-100 million crowns, no foreign partner, minority state ownership at most, and a previous failure to raise money through banks.
Privatisation is a controversial issue in Slovakia. The opposition accuses the government of cronyism while the government says the opposition was no better when it briefly held power in 1994.
The government also called off the second and final wave of mass voucher privatisation last year.

"Companies in which we would invest will be already privatised and meeting the criteria, and to me it does not make any difference how they went through privatisation," Wavre said. -- Bratislava Newsroom, 42-7-210-3687
